Nine years US Air Force, 4 Feb 1957 – 14 Feb 1966, Airman 3rd Class, “Korea, Vietnam.” Buried Chattanooga National Cemetery, Sec. Ma, Site 36. Named in his mother’s January 1983 obituary as “Robert L. Bell of Mobile, Ala.” [BELL-106] — placing him alive in Mobile that month, and confirming him as her son from a source independent of family memory. His brothers and sister are named beside him: William E. Bell of Clarkston, Ga., John H. Bell of Warner Robins, Ga., and Mrs. Carolyn B. Miller of Birmingham.
4.s: Robert Lee Bell Sr. was born in 1935 in Atlanta, Georgia — the 1940 census, read directly, corrected an old family belief that he was born in Alabama. He served nine years in the United States Air Force, from 4 February 1957 to 14 February 1966, reaching the rank of Airman 3rd Class and serving in Korea and Vietnam. He died in 2001 in Chattanooga and is buried in Chattanooga National Cemetery. Three photographs of him survive from his later years: beside a Tennessee lake in winter, out deep-sea fishing in a straw hat, and a plain portrait in a blue polo shirt. A last one, taken in a spring yard about 2000 or 2001, shows him standing with his son, his daughter-in-law and his two grandsons.

5.s: Willie Joyce Stephens was born in 1942 and died in 1982 in Jefferson County, Alabama. She married Robert Lee Bell Sr. on 26 August 1960 in Fort Payne, and later remarried John Duncan Lammon in 1980. She is buried in Clarke County among her mother's Truett family — one reason she was hard to trace for years was that she did not die under the Bell name. Three photographs of her survive, all from her last two years: her wedding to John Duncan Lammon on 24 May 1980, married at home beneath a flowered brass arch; a restaurant above the water, his arm around her shoulders; and one of her alone in a panelled room hung with framed stamp collections. They are the only known pictures of her.

6.s: Richard Clark Tuttle, known all his life as Dick, was born in 1929 in Terre Haute, Indiana, and died in 2015 in Cincinnati. He served in the US Army, enlisting at Fort Lee, Virginia, on 3 August 1951 and training there as a supply-records specialist. A photograph kept in the family shows him in uniform in Germany, standing beside the sign for the Headquarters, Heilbronn Sub Post — the first evidence of where he was actually stationed. A senior yearbook placing him in the Evanston Township High School class of 1947 pushed the family's known move north back to about 1945, five years earlier than long assumed. The earliest photograph of him shows him at about nine, in a sweater and short trousers, standing beside his older brother Robert on a patch of spring grass in Terre Haute.

8.x:
The 1940 conviction read in full [BELL-96]: sentenced 17 June 1940, twelve months, serial C 26,574, discharged 17 Oct 1940 by order of Judge Emmett Perry — a new fixed point placing him in Jefferson County that October. Weighed 163 lb; physical condition good, teeth bad. ⭐ And from the reverse of his draft card [BELL-107], a mark that could identify a body no name index will match: “knot on the left leg near the hip.” ⭐ His own 1930 census gives BOTH his parents as Alabama-born [BELL-100] — a test Thomas Jefferson Bell and Alice May Bradley pass, and one that could have failed. Documented 1901 to Jan 1944, then dark. The free online layer is now exhausted [BELL-86, BELL-87]; the live lead is a Henry Bell, 51, born Alabama, separated, lodging at the Mt. Airy home for the homeless in Cincinnati in April 1950 [BELL-85]. ⭐ Strengthened 12 Aug 2026 [BELL-99]: in the whole 1950 census of Hamilton County, Ohio he is the only white male Bell born in Alabama in that decade — one man out of 106 — and “separated” is exactly what a man who walked out in 1942 and never formalised it would say. Still unproven: the age is two years out, and the record gives no parents, no next of kin and no middle name. ⛔ Buried in neither of the two family cemeteries. Not at Forest Hill, Birmingham — his wife’s and infant daughter’s ground, all 91 Bell memorials checked, no Henry at all [BELL-102]. And not at Bethlehem. All 16 Bell memorials in the family cemetery are listed and no Henry is among them [BELL-84]. Death bracketed 24 Jan 1944 × 29 Dec 1956, well supported — TWO complete sibling enumerations omit him: his mother's obituary of 31 Dec 1956 names six surviving children [BELL-79], and his brother W. W. Bell's of 20 Oct 1960 names four sisters and a brother, singular [BELL-90]. ⚠ He had a 1940 desertion conviction and had left the state, so an estranged son could be omitted while living; strong evidence, not proof. ⭐ ADPH certificate #5206 — John H Bell, d. 27 Feb 1951, HOUSTON CO. (Dothan, his mother's town) — is the highest-value order in the project [BELL-80]. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ RE-GRADED ‘part’ → ‘ok’, 6 Aug 2026, AT ALEC’S CHALLENGE [AUDIT-01]. The colour grades WHO THIS PERSON IS AND WHOSE CHILD THEY ARE — not whether every fact about them is known. Loose ends belong in Outstanding, below, and this node has some. They do not make the ancestor uncertain. ⚠ Name-collision warning [BELL-104]: Barbour County held a SECOND, unrelated John Henry Bell — b. ~1890, eldest son of B. C. Bell, a Eufaula butcher, named in full in a 1910 probate petition. Eliminated as ours on age by eleven years against five records, but any Barbour "John Henry Bell" must be checked against that family first. THE WALL. Solid to 1940: m. Beatrice Eakens 13 May 1927, Birmingham; dry cleaner 1928, truck driver 1930, house painter 1940; in Atlanta c.1933–36. Convicted of desertion and non-support in Jefferson County 17 June 1940 (Juv. & Dom. Rel. case 6552, Judge Emmett Perry); released 17 Oct 1940. ⭐ Registered for the draft at Cincinnati on 23 February 1942 — Local Board No. 19, 1206 Baymiller Street — giving his birthplace as Barbour County, Alabama and naming Mrs. M. K. Norton of 118 North St., Dothan as the person who would always know his address. He signed it himself. It is the last document he is known to have signed.

Outstanding: ⭐ His parents are now established [BELL-117]. His death is not — bracketed 24 Jan 1944 × 29 Dec 1956 by absence from two complete sibling enumerations, with the estrangement caveat. ⚠ And no instrument names him as Tom and Alice’s son in words: he predeceased every record that lists their children, so the identification is proved indirectly. Each of his six siblings has such a document; he alone has none. ⛔ Illinois is now cleared [BELL-105] — every John and Henry Bell death in the state 1944–1956 was listed from the Illinois State Archives database, and no John or Henry Bell died in DuPage County at any point between 1916 and 1972. Bounded: given names searched exactly, and the database carries no age before 1948. Birth is settled at ~1901–02 [BELL-115]. Sources: 1901 (family compilation), 1903 (1940 census), ~1901-02 (1920 census, as TJB’s son “Henry”) — and his 1927 marriage licence blank reads “21” — ⭐ which is the majority formula, not an age: the packet’s own affidavit says “he is OVER 21 years of age,” while the bride’s “18” is exact because her age mattered legally. Both Birmingham papers that week printed “John Henry Bell, 25.” [BELL-70, BELL-115]. No county and no father’s name on any of it. Disappearance better dated Oct 1940 – Feb 1942 than “around 1942.”

10 Aug 2026 [BELL-63/64/66]: m. Margaret Beatrice Eaken Friday 13 May 1927, Birmingham (the News ran a fearless-bridegroom feature; register Vol. 108 p. 276). Truck driver for a dry-cleaner, 1348 Huntsville Rd (1930); painter, 71 Ormond Ave SE, Atlanta (1936). Named his firstborn THOMAS J. for his father — the boy died at 16 on 22 Jan 1944 after a car crash at Warrenville, Illinois — ⭐ and his death certificate puts the whole family at Wheaton, DuPage County, Illinois, a state this project had never searched [BELL-101]. It also names the father plainly as "Henry Bell", the notice naming brothers John Henry Jr., Billy Jean, “Bobby” (8) and sister Carolyn, and grandmothers Mrs. M. K. Norton and Mrs. Margaret Bloebaum. Walked out ~1942; John Henry Jr. took his SSN at fourteen (Jan 1943); no record of the father after 1942 has ever been found.

⛔ Sweep K, 12 Aug 2026 [BELL-105]: the Illinois State Archives death database (1916–1972, statewide) was searched in full. No John Bell and no Henry Bell died in DuPage County — the family’s own county in Jan 1944 — at any point across those 56 years. The one strong candidate, a John H Bell dying at Aurora, Kane Co. on 13 Mar 1944 in the very city his son died in seven weeks earlier, is refuted: age 72, b. 1871 Pembroke KY, father George Bell, race “Col”. ⭐ His draft card’s unindexed identifying mark is now transcribed — “knot on the left leg near the hip” [BELL-107] — the kind of detail that can name a man in a coroner’s or poorhouse record when no index will.
8.s:
John Henry Bell was born on 4 August 1901 in Barbour County, Alabama — a date his family still remembered in 2009, and one he wrote down himself on a draft card in 1942. He was the eldest son of Thomas Jefferson Bell and Alice May Bradley, farmers near Louisville, and he appears in their household in 1910 and 1920 simply as “Henry.”

By 1925 he had left for Birmingham, and a Barbour County court recorded him there — “Henry Bell, Birmingham” — when his grandfather’s estate was divided seven ways among Tom’s children. Two years later, on Friday the thirteenth of May 1927, he married Margaret Beatrice Eaken. Both Birmingham papers thought a couple marrying on such a date was worth a humorous column. Their first son arrived six months later.

He drove a truck for a dry cleaner, then painted houses — in Birmingham, and in Atlanta through the middle thirties. There were six children. In June 1940 he was convicted in Jefferson County of desertion and non-support, and served four months of a twelve-month sentence; the prison ledger records him at 163 pounds, physical condition good, teeth bad.

He was released that October, and about a year later he left for good. On 23 February 1942 he registered for the draft in Cincinnati — five foot nine, 160 pounds, blue eyes, brown hair, a knot on his left leg near the hip — and gave, as the person who would always know his address, his mother in Dothan. It is the last document he is known to have signed.

After that he vanishes. His family moved north to Wheaton, Illinois, where his sixteen-year-old son was killed in a car crash in January 1944; the certificate names the father simply as “Henry Bell.” By the time his mother died in December 1956 her obituary listed six surviving children, and he was not among them. He lies in neither family cemetery. The likeliest trace of him is a Henry Bell, fifty-one, white, born in Alabama and recorded as “separated,” lodging in a home for the homeless outside Cincinnati in April 1950 — the only man of that description in the entire county.

9.s:
Margaret Beatrice Eaken was born on 10 July 1908 at Cuba, in Sumter County, Alabama — her mother's home county, where her father would later be buried. She was eighteen when she married John Henry Bell on Friday the thirteenth of May 1927, and their first son was born that November.

She had six children by him. He left about 1942, and by January 1944 she had taken the family north to Wheaton, Illinois, where her eldest son was killed in a car crash at sixteen. She remarried in 1948 — Claude B. Smith — and the 1950 census finds her at Lineville, Clay County, Alabama, with her four surviving Bell children in the household.

She spent her later years in Georgia, at Clarkston, and retired from Rich's department store in Atlanta. She died on 16 January 1983, aged seventy-four, and was brought back to Birmingham for burial at Forest Hill, where her infant daughter Marion had been buried half a century before. Her obituary ran in both cities and listed her husband, her four children, her mother and her two brothers. It did not mention her first husband.

For a long time the family believed she died in 1985 — but 1985 was the year her own mother died, and the two had quietly become confused.

She married at least three times — to a Stephens in 1939, a Rivers in 1947, and later a Roberts — and appears in Social Security records under the name “Grace Tru Morgan,” suggesting a fourth marriage as well. A photograph survives of him with Helen in the early 1970s, the two of them hand in hand and wearing flowers, most likely at their fiftieth anniversary.

13.s: Helen May Knott was born on 12 June 1905 in Indiana and died on 24 April 1977 at Evanston Hospital, Illinois, at the age of seventy-one. Her parents are named on her 1923 marriage application to Gifford Tuttle, and again decades later in her son Robert Dale's obituary. Her death notice named her surviving sons, Robert D. of Evanston and Richard C. of Cincinnati, and her sister Mildred Cooper of Cedar Rapids. Three photographs survive of her childhood in Terre Haute about 1911 to 1913: one on the lawn beside her big sister Mildred, seven years her elder, which their mother sent as a postcard inscribed “My too sweet dauters, Mildred and Helen”; and two of Helen with her friend Grace, both girls in wide straw hats. The friend was almost certainly Grace Estella Schomer, born six months after Helen in December 1905, the daughter of the man who ran Terre Haute's dancing school — a child performer the local paper once called “the miniature Pavlowa.” She lived to be ninety-seven. A hand-tinted studio portrait shows her in her late thirties, and another photograph catches her with Gifford in the early 1970s, near their fiftieth anniversary.

By October 1964 he was living at 316 West Dartmouth in Flint, Michigan — a chapter of his life discovered only through his wife Velma's cremation certificate. His own death has not yet been found. The earliest picture of him is a studio photograph taken about 1903 or 1904, when he was still an infant in a long white gown, seated between his older sister and brother — Katherine and Harry, each named for a parent.

She was five feet tall, ran away from home at sixteen, and her school yearbook remembered her as “small but oh my!” She died on 3 October 1964 in Flint, Michigan, of a perforated duodenum after years of high-dose aspirin taken for arthritis. She was, for years, the hardest figure in the family to trace, until a cremation certificate found in a family photo album, together with her granddaughter Cynthia's own memory of her, finally identified her. Two photographs of her survive: a studio portrait, and a snapshot of her laughing outdoors in a plaid coat in her fifties.

16.d: b. 1875×1878 – d. 30 Aug 1921, near Louisville, Barbour Co., Alabama
16.x:
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ RE-GRADED ‘probable’ → ‘documented’, 12 August 2026, on the EIGHTH adversarial review [BELL-117] — after seven refusals. What changed: the rival reading of “Mrs. M. K. Norton” died with Katie Bradley in April 1924; Mack Norton’s own 1954 obituary calls Alice’s children Bells; and the 1925 probate decree was re-read as what it is — a court’s adjudication of who Thomas Jefferson Bell’s children were, paying seven named persons exactly one seventh each of a deceased heir’s share, with “Henry Bell, Birmingham” among them.

⭐ Corroborated from the Norton side [BELL-108]: his widow Alice remarried Mack K. Norton, whose 1954 obituary calls her sons T. R. and W. W. Bell — the same sibling set Thomas Ray Bell Sr.’s own obituary gives twenty years later, from the opposite side of the family. Mack joined Bethlehem Baptist near Clayton, this family’s church and burying ground, where Tom lies and where Alice is buried under the name Bell, not Norton.

Buried Bethlehem Baptist Church Cemetery; Find a Grave memorial 138198515 links him to John T. Bell and Sallie Cox as parents — corroboration of a hypothesis, not evidence [BELL-84]. ⚠ That memorial gives d. 27 Aug 1920 against the Clayton Record obituary's 30 Aug 1921; one is wrong by a year and the conflict is unresolved. Identified as John Henry Bell's father at probable — the chain runs through his widow, not through a document naming him [BELL-76, BELL-77]. Married Alice May Bradly 13 Aug 1895, Barbour Co. Direct Marriage Index vol. 13 p. 63. Obituary, Clayton Record 2 Sep 1921: d. 30 Aug 1921, son of John Bell Sr., buried Bethlehem “where two of his children are buried.” 1920 census, Louisville: Thomas J 44, Alice 42, Henry 18, Ray 16, William 12, Ethel 10, Juanita 2.

Outstanding: No record yet names John Henry Bell's father. His own age is unsettled — 44 in Jan 1920 (b. ~1875) against “about forty-three” in the Sept 1921 obituary (b. ~1878); the chart's old “1874” was supported by nothing. The Barbour sweep for competing Henry Bells is now RUN [BELL-82]: across the 1900, 1910 and 1920 censuses there is exactly one Henry Bell born 1899×1903 in the county, and he is Tom and Alice's son. No rival exists.
16.s:
Thomas Jefferson Bell farmed near Louisville in Barbour County, Alabama. He married Alice May Bradley on 13 August 1895, when she was eighteen, and they had nine children — seven still living when the 1920 census found them together, and two already buried at Bethlehem Baptist churchyard.

He died on 30 August 1921 and was laid beside those two children. He left no estate: the county's probate minutes for the year after his death record no administration in his name, and the clerk's index to seventy years of administrators' records contains no Thomas J. Bell at all. There was simply nothing to divide.

So when his children finally received something, it came through his own father's estate instead. In April 1925 a Barbour County court divided one deceased heir's share seven ways among Tom's children, naming each of them — Ellie, Ray, Ruth, William, Ethel, little Juanita, and “Henry Bell, Birmingham.” That decree is the court's own answer to the question of who his children were, and it is the document that finally settled this family's longest-standing puzzle.

Norton” died with Katie Bradley in April 1924; Mack Norton’s own 1954 obituary calls Alice’s children Bells; and the 1925 probate decree was re-read as what it is — a court’s adjudication of who Thomas Jefferson Bell’s children were, paying seven named persons exactly one seventh each of a deceased heir’s share, with “Henry Bell, Birmingham” among them.

⭐⭐ The Norton question is settled [BELL-108]. Mack K. Norton’s own obituary (The Clayton Record, 22 Oct 1954) names his wife as “Mrs. Alice May Norton of Dothan” and her children as step-sons T. R. Bell of Bessemer and W. W. Bell of Jacksonville, with four step-daughters whose married names and towns match Thomas Ray Bell Sr.’s own 1974 obituary twenty years later. So the “Mrs. M. K. Norton, 118 North St., Dothan” whom John Henry Bell named on his 1942 draft card is Alice — and the competing reading, that she was Katie the aunt, is dead: Katie Bradley Norton died 11 April 1924, eighteen years before that card.

⭐ And Katie was Alice’s sister. Both women’s state death records give the same parents, Henry Bradley and Elvira Loveless. Two Bradley sisters each married a Bell and each was widowed; Mack Norton married Katie in 1912 and, after she died, married Alice. Mack joined his wife’s first husband’s church at Bethlehem and was buried apart from her.

⭐ Named with Tom as a parental couple on a state vital record: their daughter Ruth's Texas death certificate gives father Tom Bell, mother Alice Bradley [BELL-91], and their son Thomas Ray's Alabama death record gives Thomas Jefferson Bell and Alice Bradley [BELL-95]. Two children, two states, two vital records. Identified at probable. Maiden name attested in the Barbour Co. marriage index: T. J. Bell × Alice May Bradly, 13 Aug 1895 [BELL-76]. 1940 census, Dothan, ED 35-8, sheet 3B, house 118 — Mack K. Norton head, Alice M. wife; supplementary line 55 gives age at first marriage 18, nine children born, and “married more than once: Yes”, which orders the two marriages Bell-then-Norton [BELL-77]. 1935 residence: same house — seven years before John Henry gave that address on his draft card. Died 29 Dec 1956, Montgomery (Alabama Death Index, cert. #26068); buried under the name Bell at Bethlehem, the cemetery Tom's 1921 obituary named [self-correction #32].

Outstanding: ⭐ ADPH certificate #26068 names HER parents — and after the 1895 licence turned out to carry no parents' line [BELL-81], it is now the ONLY live route to the Bradley generation. Her own obituary, Clayton Record late Dec 1956, would list surviving children and is the document that would take both these nodes to documented. No marriage record for Alice × Norton exists after four bounded searches; the remarriage is proven by household, not by a return. Birth year wobbles: 1877 by the 1891 guardianship, 1876 by Find a Grave, whose provenance is unverified.
17.s:
Alice May Bradley was born on 8 October 1876 in Barbour County, Alabama, the daughter of Henry Bradley and Elvira Loveless. Her father died young: in October 1891 a county court appointed a guardian for Alice, then fourteen, and her sister Katie, twelve, noting that the minors had no father living.

She married Thomas Jefferson Bell on 13 August 1895, at eighteen, and had nine children. Widowed in 1921, she married Mack K. Norton — and there is a quiet symmetry in it, because Mack's first wife had been her own sister Katie, who died in 1924. Two Bradley sisters each married a Bell, each was widowed, and the same man married them in turn.

By 1935 she was living with Mack at 118 East North Street in Dothan, and it was that address her son wrote on his draft card in 1942 when the form asked who would always know where he was. Mack died in 1954; his obituary called her children his step-sons and step-daughters, naming them as Bells, which is how the family was finally proved from the outside.

She outlived her husband by thirty-five years and died at Montgomery on 29 December 1956, aged eighty. They brought her home to Bethlehem, in Barbour County, and buried her beside him under the name Bell — not Norton.

24.s: Dennis Clark Tuttle was born on 25 January 1884 in Peoria, Illinois, and died on 22 August 1975. He worked forty-three years as a freight car repairman for the Pennsylvania Railroad, retiring onto its Roll of Honor, and was a Freemason, serving as Prophet of the Kerman Grotto in Terre Haute. He registered for the “Old Man's Draft” in April 1942 and, in his sixties, drew twenty dollars a week from Indiana unemployment during a lean stretch. He was married for sixty-seven years, and his own wallet, carried through much of that life, survives among the family's papers.

25.s: Leona Marie Alexander was born on 16 February 1883 in Clinton, Indiana, and died on 13 September 1970. Sarah Cox married John T. Bell on 7 March 1861 in Barbour County, Alabama. He was twenty; the war began the following month.

They raised a large family — at least eight sons and two daughters survived to be named in his will twenty-five years after her death — and one of those sons was Thomas Jefferson Bell. In April 1888 she signed her name beside her husband’s on a deed selling a right of way to the Eufaula & East Alabama Railway, giving up her dower in about forty-six acres of it.

She died in 1910, five years before John, and by the time his will was probated no widow was named.

John Bell was born about 1807 in South Carolina and had moved to Barbour County, Alabama before 1837, where all of his children were born. The 1850 census finds him at forty-three, farming, with his wife Laney — also South Carolina born — and five children at home.

Two of those children matter to this family: William, aged eleven, who would die a Confederate pensioner in 1924 leaving an estate that scattered across his nieces and nephews; and John, aged nine, who would become John T. Bell and father Thomas Jefferson Bell.

His son’s obituary says he came to Alabama from Darlington, South Carolina, about 1830, and settled in the neighbourhood where the family stayed for the next century. He is the point at which this line leaves Alabama — and Darlington District is where everything before him has to be looked for.

⭐⭐ Her name is LANEY, and as of 13 Aug 2026 that is a manuscript reading rather than an index transcription [BELL-149, BELL-151]. Three census images have now been rendered at native resolution and read by eye — 1850 (aged 42), 1860 (53) and 1870 (64) — in three different hands, all writing Laney. ⭐ The 1860 enumerator wrote “Post Office Louisville” in his own header and “S. Carolina” in the birthplace column of the same line: the capital in her name is his L, not his C. ⭐ The FamilySearch index reads her 1870 age as 44; the manuscript reads 64, formed like the 6 in her husband’s 63 on the line above, and that correction has been checked twice.

⭐ She is in the household before the children were born. The 1840 Barbour schedule, whose female columns were unread until now, tallies one female aged 30–40 beside John at 30–40, with one boy and one girl under five — William, born February 1839, and Mary. ⭐ Her death is dated by record: the household is intact in August 1870 and John Bell is enumerated widowed in June 1880.

⚠ Held at probable on a second adversarial review, 13 Aug 2026 [BELL-151], and the reason is precise. Everything above establishes who she was. Nothing states that she was John T. Bell’s mother in words — the schedules of 1850, 1860 and 1870 carry no relationship column, so four enumerations are one kind of evidence four times over. And the single record in this family that does name a mother — William W. Bell’s 1924 Alabama death record, certificate 4736 — calls her Viney. ⚠ Viney is a clipping of Lavinia; Laney is a clipping of Elaine or Delaney; no one name yields both, so the easy reconciliation does not exist. The live alternative is two wives, and it requires no misreading of anything.

Outstanding: ⭐ She has a grave: Find a Grave memorial 68717758, “Laney Hurst Bell,” died 17 June 1873, BEASLEY FAMILY CEMETERY, Barbour County — the same small burying ground as her son William W. Bell, on the farm that bounded theirs. ⚠ There is no photograph, the entry is contributor-made, and the surname Hurst is a hypothesis only — it is also the mother’s surname on the death record of a different C. A. Bell, so it may be a compiler’s error carried across. It is not on this chart as her name. ⭐ What would settle her: a photograph of the stone; or Alabama certificate 475 of 1915 for John T. Bell, the only document that would name his own mother; or certificate 4736 of 1924, to see whether Viney is the informant’s word or the indexer’s.
65.s:
She was born in South Carolina about 1806 and came to Alabama as a young wife. In August 1840 she is a tally mark in a column — one woman aged thirty to forty in John Bell’s house in Barbour County, with a baby boy and a little girl. In 1850 she has a name, Laney, and five children. In 1860 she is fifty-three, and the family is prosperous: her husband returns four thousand dollars in land and ten thousand in personal estate. In 1870 she is sixty-four, keeping house, with her grown daughter Mary and her son Archibald still at home, and her son John T. Bell farming the next place along with a wife and four small children.

Then she is gone. By June 1880 her husband is enumerated as a widower, living with a lodger and a girl of fourteen, his children grown and scattered. A gravestone in the Beasley family’s little burying ground is said to give the date as 17 June 1873, though no one has photographed it.

Fifty-one years after she died, her eldest son’s death certificate called her Viney. Three census-takers had called her Laney. Nobody now alive knows which she answered to.

80.s: Henry H. Stephens was born on 8 August 1822 in North Carolina and died in October 1879 in Gaston, Sumter County, Alabama. He is the best-documented man on this line, traced through census records from Sumter County, Alabama in 1850, to Newton County, Mississippi in 1860, and back to Cuba, in Sumter County, Alabama, by 1870. 88.s: John Wesley Truett was born on 20 October 1833 and died on 17 April 1914. He served as a private in Company D of the 32nd Alabama Infantry during the Civil War, enlisting on 15 October 1862 at Coffeeville, and was hospitalized within weeks with chronic rheumatism that kept him listed as absent for the rest of the war. A voucher he signed himself at Dalton, Georgia, on 30 May 1863 is the oldest surviving signature of a direct ancestor in this family's records, and he was later enumerated, at age 73, in the 1907 Alabama Census of Confederate Veterans.

128.d: b. about 1770–1775; d. before 22 October 1839, Sumter District, South Carolina
128.x:
⭐⭐ A candidate with a documented life and no document tying him to us. He is graded hypothesis deliberately — but for a narrower reason than this node used to give. ⭐ Archy Bell’s own will names a son JOHN BELL: “the remainder I will & bequeath to my beloved children to be equally divided between them, viz, John Bell, Celey Amoson, Harriett Bell, Martha Bell, William Wesley Bell, and Jane Bell” — verified in the signed original, the clerk’s certified copy and the recorded will book [BELL-430]. ⚠ What is NOT documented is that this son John is OUR John F. Bell of Barbour County, Alabama. The open question is an identification, not a relationship — and a “John Bell Senr” was witnessing deeds in Darlington in 1820, so uniqueness cannot be assumed. What follows is the case, which is now a strong one.

⭐ He left a will [BELL-147]. Made 4 October 1839 and filed at Sumter District on the 22nd, it leaves his wife Margaret the 275-acre plantation for her life or widowhood, then to five children — Benjamin Sumter, Margaret Louisa, Ezekiel Dixon, Hugh McCallum and Columbus Campbell Bell. An 1846 partition establishes that those five are the children of a second marriage. The residue he leaves to six more: ⭐ “John Bell, Celey Amoson, Harriet Bell, Martha Bell, William Wesley Bell, and Jane Bell.”

⭐ That earlier family is dated, and it is dated to the right decade. William Wesley Bell is in the 1850 Darlington census aged 30, born 1820 [BELL-160]. So the six were born roughly 1805×1820 — the window in which John Bell was born, 13 January 1807, and the window of Archibald’s marriage to Martha, who released dower in 1809 and 1817.

⭐⭐ And his household held a boy of exactly the right age, twice [BELL-159]. The 1820 Sumter schedule (page 115, indexed “Arel Bell”) tallies one male aged 10 and under 16 — John was thirteen. The 1830 schedule (page 66, indexed “Achable Bell”) tallies one male aged 20 and under 30 — John was twenty-three, and his family left for Alabama “about 1830.” Archibald himself is 45-and-upwards in 1820 and 50–60 in 1830. ⚠ But the bracket is not exclusive: of the seven Bell households on the 1830 Sumter schedule, the elder John Bell’s (p. 93) also holds an anonymous male 20–30 [BELL-166] — the census cannot choose between the two roofs.

⭐ The neighbours run for twenty-six years. Robert Severance is the household directly below him in 1820, sells him land in 1836, and his estate bounds Archibald’s farm in 1846. William Copeland is on the 1830 page and witnesses the will. The Amosons are on both pages, and a daughter married one of them.

Outstanding — and these are the reasons the grade has not moved [BELL-148, BELL-162]: ⛔ No instrument names John Bell as his son, and none places the will’s John Bell in Alabama. The estate packet was opened in August 2026 and contains no legatee receipts at all. ⛔ Two other Sumter Bell households in 1820 — Thomas Bell, on the line immediately above him, and John Bell — also held a boy of John’s age, and if those men are his brothers then the rivals are his nephews, sharing every neighbour and every migration route. ⛔ And the rival persists: in 1830 the elder John Bell’s household (the probable “John Bell Senr” of the 1839 bond) still holds a male 20–30, while Thomas Bell’s household has vanished from the schedule entirely, leaving his boy unlocated [BELL-166]. ⚠ The Darlington-vs-Sumter question has narrowed sharply: beyond the shared “Archy”/“Archibald” usage and the three surnames that cross the creek with him (Huggins, Chaney, Newman), the February 1839 resurvey of his own home plantation — the Sumter estate tract itself — is headed “South Carolina, DARLINGTON DISTRICT” by the deputy surveyor [BELL-170]. His home paperwork crossed the line; a single instrument equating the two men in words is still wanting. ⚠ The 1820 and 1830 tallies also leak by one boy, which is unexplained. ⭐ And the exclusion now runs one way [BELL-172]: no John Bell of the will’s generation is documentable in Sumter or Darlington District in 1840 or 1850 — the one right-age Sumter candidate resolves to James P. Bell by his own will — so the will’s John left the home districts, and ours is the only located right-age John with any documented tie to them.

⭐ 22 Aug 2026 [BELL-484]: the Darlington Archibald (wife Martha, 1809–1820) and the Sumter Archy (wife Margaret by 7 Oct 1829) are now one man stated in the record — “Archd Bell of the district of Sumpter” buying the Darlington tract on 4 May 1810, and “Archey Bell … Margaret Bell the wife of the within named Archibald Bell” on one 1829 deed. His Boykin land came “sold to said A. Bell by General Cantey” — a purchase, not a descent from William Rasor Bell. He witnessed for Jonathan Newman of Sumter District in 1805 and beside a John Bell Senr in 1820 — association, never kinship. Still no document ties him to W.R.B.’s son Archibald; the estate bundle (Sumter Box 10 Pkg 3) was opened the same week — nine leaves, no division, no receipts [BELL-485].

⭐ [BELL-485]: his own estate packet is found (Sumter Bundle 113 Pkg 15): the original signed will of 4 Oct 1839 names wife Margaret, five younger children (Benjamin Sumter, Margaret Louisa, Ezekiel Dixon [#238 — not “Nixon”], Hugh McCallum, Columbus Campbell) and six older (John, Celey Amoson, Harriett, Martha, William Wesley, Jane) — and no father or brother; the sale bill shows the family buying its household back; J. W. Stuckey was guardian ad litem for the three youngest in 1846–47. William Rasor Bell’s own bundle is nine leaves with no division or receipts, the Ordinary’s books of 1809–39 were never filmed, and Sumter equity 1795–1870 holds no Bell partition — so the document that would tie 128 to 256 is not online anywhere now searched.

⭐⚠ 24 Aug 2026 [BELL-502–503, #229]: Archy is now documented holding and mortgaging (1815, to Zachariah Cantey) the 345-acre Lynches Creek tract whose 1785 survey was laid out for William Rasor Bell — the first document putting him on node 256’s ground — but a seventh adversary pass [BELL-512] kept the link at hypothesis: W.R.B. never owned the tract (a locative recital, not a title — and the recital’s companion word is now settled as HARRISON at the ink, an inherited 1780s adjoiner call, not a plat call [BELL-517]), Archy was a serial open-market buyer, and land never conveyed keeps its dead owner’s name for decades.

The decisive documents are now all offline and named; the grade holds where seven adversaries left it.
128.s:
Archibald Bell — “Archy” to the clerks who wrote down his name — was born about 1770 to 1775, and if the reconstruction holds he was a son of William Rasor Bell, a planter of Salem in Sumter District who died leaving nine sons and a widow named Mary.

He farmed on both banks of Lynches Creek, the water that divides Sumter District from Darlington. He bought land in Darlington in 1806 and sold a hundred and twenty-seven acres there in 1817, between Bay Branch and Newmans Swamp; he was witnessing deeds across the creek in Sumter as early as 1812. His wife Martha released her dower twice, in 1809 and 1817, before a justice named John Huggins — whose family would later marry into his.

Martha died, and he married Margaret, and had five more children with names that read like a roll-call of his neighbours: Benjamin Sumter, Ezekiel Dixon, Hugh McCallum, Columbus Campbell. He was sued in 1830 for a witness fee. He was still buying land from Robert Severance in 1836, at sixty. He died in the autumn of 1839, weak in body but of sound mind, leaving two hundred and seventy-five acres, a set of blacksmith’s tools, thirteen geese, and a boy named Limus whom he directed to be sold to pay his debts.

Whether the John Bell he named first among his older children is the John Bell who went to Alabama about 1830 is the question this family has not yet answered.

129.d: wife of Archibald Bell by October 1809; living February 1817, Darlington District, South Carolina
129.x:
⭐ “Martha Bell, the wife of the above named Archibald Bell” appeared twice before a Darlington District justice of the peace — 17 October 1809 and 24 February 1817 — and, examined privately and separately from her husband as the law required of a married woman, released her dower in land he was selling. In 1809 she made her mark. ⭐ The 1809 record, found 13 Aug 2026 [BELL-150], moves her eight years earlier than this file had her, and closes the gap between her documented marriage and John Bell’s birth in January 1807 to under three years.

⚠ She is the weaker of these two nodes and must be judged separately from her husband [BELL-148, BELL-162]. For Martha to be John Bell’s mother, three things must all hold: that the Darlington Archibald and the Sumter Archy are one man; that Martha was the first of his wives; and that the earlier family in his will is hers.

Outstanding: ⛔ No source anywhere states that Martha was the mother of anybody. ⛔ Every document naming her is a Darlington instrument, while every document of the will and the estate is Sumter — so she depends entirely on a merge that is still undocumented. ⚠ His 1839 will names a wife Margaret, and “children by his second marriage” establishes at least two marriages, not exactly two; a Martha who was wife number two of three, and stepmother rather than mother to the older children, fits every record equally well. ⚠ The 1830 Sumter schedule shows the woman of that house aged 30–40, who would have been only nine to nineteen in 1809 — so she is probably Margaret, and Martha is probably already dead. Her maiden name and her dates are unknown.

⭐ [BELL-484]: Martha living 20 Sept 1820 (dower, Sumter); Margaret is Archibald’s wife by 7 Oct 1829 (dower, Sumter) — the change falls 1820×1829, not c.1830.
129.s:
Martha Bell appears twice, briefly. In October 1809, and again in February 1817, her husband Archibald sold land in Darlington District, South Carolina, and each time she came before a justice of the peace — the same man both times, John Huggins — who examined her privately and separately from her husband, as the law required, to be sure a wife was not signing away her dower under his eye. She declared she did it freely and voluntarily, without compulsion, dread or fear of any person whomsoever. In 1809 she made her mark.

That is all we have of her, and whether she was John Bell’s mother is a hypothesis resting on her husband’s.

144.s: Joseph Eakins died in early 1805 in New Hanover County, North Carolina. In 1790 he bought 400 acres on Moores Creek, described in the deed as a "Gentleman," sold that land in 1793, and in 1796 received a 210-acre North Carolina state land grant signed by Governor Samuel Ashe. After his death, his widow's year's provision was allotted in March 1805 and his goods were sold at auction that April for $1,657.57. The Eakins family cemetery still stands on land he once owned, with burials dating from 1797 to the present day.

160.s:
Moore Stephens was born about 1796 in North Carolina and was still living in Sumter County, Alabama, in 1850, later moving on to Newton County, Mississippi. He married Rebecca Moize on 3 September 1817 in Orange County, North Carolina, and the two were still together, and still recorded as North Carolina-born, in both the 1850 and 1860 census. He was one of ten heirs at law of Mary Thorn's 1846 Greene County, Alabama estate, alongside nine named siblings — William, Lewis, Charles, and James Stephens, and sisters Nancy Barnett, Mary Barnett, Lucinda Ball, Elizabeth Beavers, and Esther Hitt.

After his sister Esther's death, he and Rebecca raised her two orphaned children alongside their own, naming a daughter Easter in her memory. The 1850 slave schedule for Sumter County records that Moore held one enslaved person, an unnamed Black girl about seven years old.

192.s:
Colonel Gershom Tuttle III was born on 11 June 1769 and died on 5 September 1823. According to the 1883 Tuttle genealogy, he moved from Bristol, Connecticut, to Paris in Oneida County, New York, about 1790, and then around 1800 to Jefferson County, New York, where he opened a 275-acre farm near what became Watertown. He was one of the town's first highway commissioners, helped build the first grist mill in the town of Rutland in 1806, and opened a tavern on the main highway to the lake country that became famous during the War of 1812, in which he served as Lieutenant Colonel of the 76th New York Militia, a regiment that bore his name.

He married Pamelia Strong Clark on 8 July 1788 in Farmington, Connecticut, and the family later removed to Vigo County, Indiana, in 1816, where he served as county commissioner from 1820. He was described by his contemporaries as a man of excellent character and genial temper, fond of a joke and a capital storyteller, and he is buried at Otter Creek Union Cemetery, North Terre Haute, in Vigo County, Indiana.

193.s:
Pamelia Strong Clark was born on 4 November 1770 in Farmington, Connecticut, and died on 15 April 1851, by one account, or 15 November 1851 by another — sources disagree on the exact date — near Nashville, Indiana. She married Gershom Tuttle on 8 July 1788 in Farmington; according to the 1883 Tuttle genealogy, her brother was a United States Army officer who died while commanding the U.S. arsenal at Troy, New York, and her nephew was General Newman Strong Clark of the Department of the Pacific.

She outlived her husband by twenty-eight years, following one of their children south, and is buried at Southview Cemetery in Nashville, Brown County, Indiana, ninety miles from where he lies. Her middle name, Strong, was carried on through her descendants for four generations, though a search of the standard genealogy of the Strong family has so far failed to confirm any direct Strong ancestry for her.

Outstanding: ⛔ This node is on the chart at Alec’s direction and stands or falls with node 128 — no document yet ties OUR John Bell to Archibald, so everything above Archibald is conditional on that link. ⛔ His own parents are unidentified; the leading frame is the Raccoon Swamp Bell clan of Albemarle Parish, Surry/Sussex Co., Virginia — narrowed hard on 14 Aug 2026: Rev. James Bell’s will (Sussex WB C p.310, proved 15 Oct 1778) was read off the will book and names six children — no William, no Frederick, no Lewis — ELIMINATING the patriarch’s heir-branch [BELL-193]. Hannah Bell’s will (WB B p.153, proved 17 Mar 1768) reveals the two places a father can still hide: an unnamed SON WHO DIED before 1765 (father of grandsons Silvanus & Zadock Bell), and an ABSENT son Benjamin — “provided he comes himself in person” — gone from Virginia by 1765 [BELL-194]. The patriarch’s own 1746 will, read the same day [BELL-196], names FIVE sons — John Jr., Burrell, Benjamin, Balaam, James — no William in the clan’s senior generation; if WRB belongs here it is as an unnamed grandson via BURRELL or BALAAM — the adversary-verified register work [BELL-197, BELL-199] closed John Jr.’s issue at two sons (Sylvanus & John, by PHOEBE STOKES — Micajah’s sister), and found the second dead son: Balaam Bell d. 1755, widow Mary, posthumous daughter Phoebe — his 1745×55 window fits WRB’s birth. Silvanus STOKES Junr witnessed the 1746 will — the Stokes intimacy begins in Virginia, a generation before WRB’s kinship-language settlement on Micajah Stokes’s children. Otherwise the descent runs outside the clan, e.g. Richard Bell of Lawne's Creek, d. 1734, whose sons include a William [BELL-183–185, BELL-191, BELL-196]. ⛔ The “Rasor” name — likely his mother’s or grandmother’s family — has no located source; no Rasor appears in the parish register. ⭐ His own Patriot case is ONE PRINTED INDENT — Book G No. 30, “Issued the 22d. April 1784 To Mr. William Bell for Eleven pounds Eight Shillings and Seven pence Sterling for two Horses impressed for Militia Use in October 1780.” It is the only William Bell indent in South Carolina unattributed to any man, and no DAR or SAR lineage claims it. ⚠ Nothing yet ties its claimant to him rather than to one of at least six other South Carolina William Bells, and the Chester “W:m Bell Sen:r” is not excluded. Frederick’s is now PROBABLE: three indents incl. 50 days at the Siege of Charleston in Capt. John Nelson’s company — a company three pensioners place in the Black River / Salem country of old Camden District [BELL-192, BELL-195].

⭐⭐ Where the case stood after the sweep of 19–20 August 2026 [BELL-382–406]. Book G No. 30 survived three separate attempts to take it off the board in four days and remains unseated and unexcluded. What strengthened: the printed text was transcribed from the surviving counterfoil itself — Wates’s asterisk/dagger marks are a survival map, Book G’s stubs go missing only from No. 251, and No. 30 is unmarked, 220 entries inside the intact run [BELL-385]. The evidence type is pre-approved with an exact precedent: DAR ancestor A008802 carries 46 approved lineages on a single stub-entry citation [BELL-392]. The rival Abbeville claimant is now excluded on his own itemised schedule, and the Chester man’s claims fell from three to two — one of them proved to be William Ball — so £11.8.7 no longer sits between his sums but above both [BELL-395]. What was closed off: no second October-1780 impressment claim exists anywhere in the twelve printed volumes [BELL-384, BELL-391]; his neighbours left six indents between them in 12,242, so no cohort argument can be built [BELL-394]; and the numbered Treasury returns were alphabetical work-batches, never geographic [BELL-396]. Book G No. 30 is cited by nobody in either lineage society, checked against the full source citation of every South Carolina Bell in both [BELL-392].

⭐ And his own paper trail was pushed back and sharpened. There is no South Carolina record of him before 1785, tested across seven name-forms — the apparent 1777/1778 hits are index frames carrying the 1785 judgment roll [BELL-400, BELL-406]. He has two 1785 surveys, not one: 150 acres on Bane Branch, 30 April, and 400 acres on Lynches Creek, 15 June — and both grants issued to Samuel Boykin, who paid the treasury fee, which was the local norm [BELL-400]. ⭐ His own plat survives and is cited to the page — Surveyor-General, Land Plats vol. 9Q p. 383 — and the Surveyor-General’s own index dates it 30 April 1784, a year before the grant’s recital. Volume 9Q is one of six Q-volumes never microfilmed; it is the arbiter of whether his South Carolina floor is 1784 or 1785 [BELL-406]. The Micajah Stokes transaction is four instruments over two days in April 1787, including a gift of land to a seventh child, Drury Stokes, not previously known [BELL-406]. ⚠ Origin, still hypothesis: a royal warrant of January 1773 lays out Duplin County, North Carolina land to Fredrick Bell “on the S. side of Bare Swamp joining his own & W:m Rasor Bells Line” — read at the ink, and it is a Bell, not a Ball. Frederick Bell is documented in Camden District, South Carolina on 8 May 1777 [BELL-404], so the brother’s crossing is proved; William’s is not. ⛔ The survey run on that same warrant fourteen months later names a different neighbour, so his entire North Carolina footprint is one clause in one clerk’s hand [BELL-397, BELL-402].

He farmed the Black River country beside Frederick Bell and the Newmans, proved deeds across the line in Darlington, and on the day after Christmas 1803, “very sick & weak in body,” divided a plain farmer’s world — a plantation, stock, feather beds, a cow already called his daughter Elizabeth’s — among a wife, two daughters and nine sons, the second of whom was Archibald.

321.d: widow of James Thorn; d. shortly before 23 Jan 1844, Greene Co., Alabama
321.x:
⭐⭐⭐ STEPHENS-21, folded into the chart 7 August 2026 — the strongest indication yet that she was a SECOND WIFE whose own next of kin were Stephenses.

The final settlement of James Thorn’s estate, Greene Co., Alabama Orphans’ Court Minutes, 14 October 1844 (p. 274), distributes his legacies to Jesse W. Thorn, Nazareth Thorn, James Thorn, William Henry Thorn and Elizabeth Crisp, plus the seven children of a predeceased son Kennedy Thorn. ⭐ Mary Thorn is not among the legatees — as widow she took a widow’s share, a different thing — and the Thorn sons formally released all claims against her estate, which was administered by a STEPHENS. Had she been their mother, her estate would have gone to them and no Stephens would have been appointed to it.

⚠⚠ A strong indication, not a proof. This node stays a hypothesis. ⭐ But it dates the document that should name JANE: Mary was James Thorn’s widow, so he died first, and Jane must have come to Mary out of his estate at the assignment of the widow’s share — a proceeding that itemises people by name and value. Greene County, probably 1841–1843.

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ SHE HAD A HUSBAND, AND HE IS NAMED — 7 Aug 2026 [STEPHENS-20]. Greene County Orphans’ Court Minutes 1839–1845, ark 3:1:3Q9M-C91H-HSD8-M, image 723, page 274, 14 October 1844: “This day came Jesse W Thorn and William H Thorn administrators with the will annexed of JAMES THORN deceased … and JAMES STEPHENS administrator of the Estate of MARY THORN deceased (WHO WAS THE WIDOW OF THE SAID JAMES THORN) also appearing in open Court … the said James Stephens administrator as aforesaid acknowledge satisfaction in full of THE SHARE OF THE SAID WIDOW, his said intestate, to the estate of the said James Thorn deceased, and the said Jesse W Thorn and William H Thorn … release and discharge all claim or claims which they have or hold against the Estate of the said Mary Thorn deceased.” ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ AND THIS BEARS ON THE VERY DOUBT WRITTEN INTO THIS NODE. The outstanding note has said for days: “NO document yet uses the word ‘children.’ A childless woman’s next of kin can be nephews and nieces.” She now turns out to be a woman who died bearing the surname THORN BY MARRIAGE, whose next of kin are all named STEPHENS. The most economical explanation is that STEPHENS was her FIRST married name and THORN her second — which would make Moore, James, Lewis, William, Esther, Lucinda and Elizabeth her CHILDREN by the first marriage, exactly as the ten equal shares and Esther Hitt’s per stirpes “Representatives” already suggested. ⚠⚠ STRENGTHENED, NOT PROVED. The alternative survives: Stephens could be her MAIDEN name and the Stephens heirs her brothers and their families. The node stays ‘hyp’ until a document says so. ⭐⭐⭐ AND THE TWO DOCUMENTS THAT WOULD SETTLE IT ARE NOW NAMED AND LOCATABLE: ① a marriage of MARY STEPHENS to JAMES THORN (Greene Co., Ala., or earlier in Orange Co., North Carolina, where Moore Stephens married in 1817); ② JAMES THORN’S WILL — the court calls his administrators “with the will annexed,” so a will exists, and a will names a wife and usually her children. ⭐ NEW NAMES: JESSE W. THORN and WILLIAM H. THORN, his administrators and very likely his sons. ⚠⚠⚠ AND IT REACHES JANE. Mary’s estate was paid the widow’s share of James Thorn’s estate. In Alabama in 1844 a widow’s share of an estate that held people WAS people. JANE — sold out of Mary’s estate on 29 April 1844 for $700 [STEPHENS-13] — may well have come to Mary out of JAMES THORN’S estate, and his WILL is the first document that could name her before the sale. ——— Earlier note: NEW NODE, 6 Aug 2026 — and NOT yet proved. The Greene County Orphans’ Court cited Moore, James, Lewis and William Stephens, Esther Hitt, Lucinda Ball and Elizabeth Bevers as her NEXT OF KIN on 23 Jan 1844 [STEPHENS-07], and distributed her estate among TEN heirs in equal shares in 1846 [STEPHENS-06]. Three of the sisters are proved born Stephens by their own Greene County marriage records [STEPHENS-08], and Esther Hitt’s share went per stirpes to her “Representatives” — the treatment a court gives a predeceased CHILD. ⭐ She held promissory notes on Charles Stephens ($15.13, $32.40) and Lewis Stephens ($100) — she was banking her sons [STEPHENS-12]. ⭐ Her inventory of 27 Apr 1844 lists her whole world down to an 18-cent umbrella and a woman’s saddle — and “1 Negro woman JANE — 475.00,” worth more than everything else combined [STEPHENS-11].

Outstanding: ⚠⚠ NO document yet uses the word “children.” A childless woman’s next of kin can be nephews and nieces. She is drawn here as a HYPOTHESIS. The petition to sell land, or a Stephens × Thorn marriage, would settle it. ⚠⚠⚠ JANE, 6 Aug 2026 — FOUND: the account of sales reads “1 Negro Woman Jane ... James Stephens ... 700.00,” sold 29 April 1844 to the administrator, Moore’s own brother [STEPHENS-13]. She was 65% of the whole estate ($700 of $1,075.86), so roughly $70 of Moore’s $107.39 share was her price. In 1850 James Stephens held 13 people in Greene Co.; Jane is very probably the 38-year-old woman, but that schedule names no one [STEPHENS-14]. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ HER NAME IS ON THE OUTSIDE OF THE FILE [STEPHENS-19]: the clerk endorsed the packet “1105 · Greene County, Ala. · 1 NEGRO WOMAN JANE · Inventory of Notes · Estate file · Thorn, Mary · 1844 · James Stephens, administrator.” Everything Mary Thorn owned was summarised in two lines on the wrapper, and the first line is Jane. ⛔⛔ The packet is now BOUNDED — images 591–600, all read. The HIRE BOND and any PETITION TO SELL LAND are NOT in the loose papers (601 starts an 1825 estate; 589 is an 1861 guardian bond). Both must be sought in the GREENE CO. ORPHANS’ COURT MINUTE BOOKS 1844–46. ⚠ And the land was sold at the ordinary sale (Andrew Norwood, $127.09) — so a separate petition may never have existed, in which case this node may not be movable off ‘hyp’ by that route at all. Still owed: the 1870 census of Greene & Sumter Cos. for Jane.
321.s: Mary Thorn, also spelled Thorne, was the widow of James Thorn of Greene County, Alabama, and died shortly before 23 January 1844. She is believed to have been born a Stephens and to have been the mother, by an earlier marriage, of ten children — Moore, James, Lewis and William Stephens, and daughters Esther Hitt, Lucinda Ball and Elizabeth Bevers — who inherited her estate in equal shares. Among her possessions was an enslaved woman named Jane, sold for $700 in April 1844, easily the largest part of everything she owned. The tie between Mary and these ten Stephens children is a strong hypothesis rather than a settled fact, since no surviving document actually calls them her children.

⭐⭐ This settles two long-running conflicts in this project. The birth year is 1738, not 1739 — the DAR and the Farmington birth record agree. And he died at Watertown, New York, not in Indiana; the Otter Creek burial belongs to his son the colonel. ⚠ One small gap survives: the Farmington register was read here as 22 August, the DAR says 23rd. Settle it from the register image before the SAR application is filed.

⭐ Eight of the DAR’s nineteen approved applications on this patriot descend through exactly our couple — “child GERSHOM, spouse PARMELIA STRONG CLARK” — including National No. 536770, which is the record copy already sitting in the frozen SAR Evidence folder [SAR_32]. The other nine descend through his son Solomon.

⚠ NUMBERED 6 Aug 2026 at Alec’s correction — he is GERSHOM II, between his father Ensign Gershom I (node 768, d. 1777) and his son Col. Gershom III (node 192, d. 1823). The 1777 headstone [TUTTLE-33] is his FATHER’S, not his — this man died 5 January 1818, forty-one years later. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ HIS BIRTH RECORD FOUND 6 Aug 2026, AND IT NAMES A FATHER: “Gershom Tuttle, birth 22 August 1738, Farmington, Hartford, Connecticut — Father’s Name: GERSHOM TUTTLE” [TUTTLE-15]. ⚠ Our notes said 23 Aug 1739 Bristol; the record says 22 Aug 1738 Farmington. Bristol IS Farmington — Bristol was the parish of New Cambridge inside Farmington township until 1785, which is exactly how the 1757 Deerfield marriage styles him. The place is confirmed, not contradicted; the YEAR 1739 in our notes is probably wrong. THE PATRIOT. A conductor of teams. On 23 May 1780 the Connecticut General Assembly paid him £285.13.8 in wages and £60.13.11 for forage IN ADVANCE, and still owed him £200.2.8; he is listed first of nine conductors. The operation: 3,000 barrels of provisions — 500 tons — hauled from Connecticut into New York State, averaging 115 miles. DAR ancestor A131791. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ 6 Aug 2026 — ENTRY 9251 OF THE 1883 GENEALOGY, IN FULL [TUTTLE-30]: “Gershom Tuttle, b. Aug. 28, 1738; d. Gershom, b. Aug. 22, 1738”, and the Farmington town record says 22 August. The town record wins; the printed 28 is the book’s error and is logged, not dropped. ⭐ The New Hampshire stage is new, and Clinton/Oneida is now confirmed from a second direction.

Outstanding: ⚠⚠ A LIVE CONFLICT ON HIS DEATH PLACE. SAR evidence file 04 — the 1883 Tuttle genealogy p.511 — says he died “on his son’s farm,” Otter Creek, Vigo Co., Indiana. Find a Grave 85146147, citing our own DAR number, says Watertown, Jefferson Co., New York, burial UNKNOWN. SAR file 29 was assembled specifically to document the conflict, so it predates this project. ⚠ The same 1883 work misprints Clark Strong Tuttle’s county, so it is capable of this error. ⚠ Note too that Clark was a MILLER at Otter Creek, not a farmer. UNRESOLVED.
384.s:
Gershom Tuttle II, remembered as "the Patriot," was born 22 August 1738 in Farmington, Connecticut (in the New Cambridge parish, now Bristol), and died 5 January 1818. During the Revolutionary War he served as a teamster, conducting wagon trains of army provisions — an operation that hauled some 3,000 barrels of supplies, roughly 500 tons, from Connecticut into New York State. The Connecticut General Assembly paid him for this service in 1780, and he is recognized today as Daughters of the American Revolution Patriot Ancestor A131791.

He married Tabitha Mitchell at Deerfield, Massachusetts, on 22 December 1757. The couple later moved first to New Hampshire, then to Clinton in Oneida County, New York, and finally to Watertown, New York, where Gershom served as the first deacon of the town's first Congregational church, organized in 1803.

768.d: b. 11 Aug 1714 Wallingford – Chippens Hill, New Cambridge – d. 13 Aug 1777, Claremont, N.H.
768.x:
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ THE RANK CONFLICT IS RESOLVED, AND HIS EXACT NEIGHBOURHOOD IS NAMED — 6 Aug 2026 [TUTTLE-39]. Miscellaneous Notes on New England Families, continuing: “On his return from the north, Gershom Tuttle joined THE COLONY OF PEOPLE FROM CHESHIRE AND VICINITY who removed to the town of Farmington and settled on CHIPPEN’S HILL, in what was called New Cambridge and is now the town of Bristol. There he had his home and was prominent in church and town affairs. HE SERVED IN THE FRENCH AND INDIAN WARS AND IS CALLED ENSIGN GERSHOM TUTTLE.” ⭐⭐ THAT SETTLES THE CONFLICT LOGGED IN TUTTLE-33. The gravestone calls him ENSIGN; the 1883 book calls him “Capt. of the train-band”. The Ensign’s commission came from the FRENCH AND INDIAN WARS, not the local militia — so the stone is recording war service, and the two titles are two different things. ⭐ NEW RESEARCH TARGET: the Connecticut French and Indian War rolls, c.1755–1762. ⭐⭐⭐ AND IT EXPLAINS THE 1742 PETITION GROUP. He did not drift to Farmington — he went with a COLONY of Cheshire people, which is why Simon Tuttle and the other names on that petition [TUTTLE-20/23] are the same names as the Cheshire records. They moved as a body, and Chippen’s Hill is where they landed. ⚠⚠⚠ AND A LEAD FLAGGED, NOT WRITTEN AS A FINDING. The manuscript continues: “As is well known there was much dissention there in New Cambridge before and during the Revolutionary War. CHIPPENS HILL WAS A CENTER OF EPISCOPALIAN AND ‘TORY’ FEELING. Many of the families…” — and the transcript breaks off there. ⚠ DO NOT DRAW THE OBVIOUS CONCLUSION. Two facts already on this chart point in opposite directions: his son Gershom II is a DOCUMENTED PATRIOT (DAR A131791, paid by the Connecticut Assembly in 1780), and a Simon Tuttle was one of ten men who in 1747 “publikly declared themselves of the Church of England” at New Cambridge [TUTTLE-20]. Read the next page of the manuscript before a word of this goes in as fact. ——— Earlier note: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ “CARLETON” IS SOLVED, AND IT IS ARLINGTON — 6 Aug 2026 [TUTTLE-38]. Miscellaneous Notes on New England Families (FS film #007549089, ark 3:1:3QS7-89DX-THK7) — a manuscript that had already solved this problem and cites its sources: “Gershom Tuttle was the son of Timothy Tuttle and his wife THANKFUL DOOLITTLE, and was born in Wallingford, Aug. 11, 1714 (Wallingford Vitals, vol. 2, p. 799). … As a young man Gershom Tuttle removed from Wallingford to northern Massachusetts, where he took up THE LAND WHICH HIS FATHER TIMOTHY TUTTLE HAD OBTAINED IN THE NEW TOWN OF ARLINGTON, JUST ABOVE NORTHFIELD (which later became WINCHESTER, NEW HAMPSHIRE). During the time he was up there he evidently stayed some time in NORTHFIELD (where HIS UNCLE THE REV. BENJAMIN DOOLITTLE was the Pastor of the church) and Sunderland, somewhat farther south. There, in Sunderland, Mass., Gershom Tuttle married, Oct. 17, 1737, LOIS ALLIS (from Sunderland Town records, as given in the History of Sunderland). She was the daughter of WILLIAM ALLIS of Sunderland…” ⭐ The clerk’s hand read “Carleton” and “Earlenton” — it is ARLINGTON, and the flag on that one word was worth keeping. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ AND THE MOVE WAS KINSHIP, NOT SPECULATION. His father held the proprietor’s right; his MOTHER’S BROTHER was the minister twenty miles down the road at Northfield; he lodged with his uncle and married a girl from Sunderland. That also confirms THANKFUL DOOLITTLE as his mother from a third independent direction — this compiler calls Rev. Benjamin Doolittle his UNCLE. ⭐⭐⭐ AND IT MAKES HIS LIFE A SHAPE: Arlington became WINCHESTER, NEW HAMPSHIRE — so the frontier township he settled at twenty-two was in what is now New Hampshire, and he died in New Hampshire, at Claremont, forty-one years later. He went north twice, and the second time he stayed. ⭐ AND WE NOW HAVE THE CITATION FOR HIS BIRTH ENTRY: WALLINGFORD VITALS, VOL. 2, PAGE 799. ——— Earlier note: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ THE DEED READ AT THE PAGE — 6 Aug 2026 [TUTTLE-37]. FamilySearch ark 3:1:3QS7-89ZD-JW67, image 445 of 849, Hampden/Springfield, Massachusetts Land Records 1735–1737: “Know all Men by these presents that I TIMOTHY TUTTLE of Wallingford in the County of New Haven and Colony of Connecticutt in New England, for divers good causes and considerations and perticularly for LOVE, GOOD WILL AND FATHERLY AFFECTION that I have and [bear] to MY SON GERSHOM TUTTLE of Carleton in the County of Hampshire and province of the Massachusetts Bay in New England, have therefore given, granted and firmly pass over … unto him my said son Gershom Tuttle and to his heirs and assigns forever ALL MY RIGHT OF LAND IN SAID [CARLETON], as well that which is already laid out and all other Divisions that shall be hereafter in said TOWNSHIP on my said RIGHT to be laid out and surveyed … I am the True, Sole and Lawfull owner of the above given and Granted premises … to Warrant, Secure and Defend him the said Gersham Tuttle…” ‘Fatherly affection’ is the standard phrase of a New England gift deed, and it is the plainest statement of parentage the period produces. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ AND IT REWRITES THE ORDER OF EVENTS. He is already “of … the County of HAMPSHIRE, Massachusetts” in 1736 — a year and more BEFORE he married Lois Allis at Sunderland in October 1737. He did not go north because of the deed; he was already there, and his father signed his own share over to him. Sunderland, Hatfield and Montague — the whole Allis country — are in that same county. So the marriage is not a mystery any more: he was a young man on the Massachusetts frontier who married a local girl. ⚠⚠ WHAT “CARLETON” IS, IS STILL OPEN — and the deed itself narrows it hard. It is a TOWNSHIP in which Timothy held a PROPRIETOR’S RIGHT, with later divisions still to be laid out — that is the signature of one of the NEW MASSACHUSETTS TOWNSHIPS granted in 1735, not an old settled town. The transcript renders the name twice and differently (“Carleton”, “Earlenton”), so the clerk’s hand is ambiguous. Identify it against the 1735 Hampshire County township grants and the proprietors’ records — that will say exactly where he was living at 22. ——— Earlier note: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ THE LAST UNDOCUMENTED LINK IN THE TUTTLE LINE IS CLOSED — 6 Aug 2026 [TUTTLE-36]. A DEED OF GIFT OF 1736 IN WHICH TIMOTHY TUTTLE CALLS GERSHOM HIS SON, TWICE. FamilySearch full-text, Springfield, Hampden, Massachusetts. Land Records 1734-1735, 1735-1737, 1736-1744, YEARS: 1736, nine matched passages — “…presents that I TIMOTHY TUTTLE OF WALLINGFORD in …” · “…and are to my SON GERSHOM TUTTLE of Carleton in …” · “…unto him my said son Gershom Tuttle and to his …” · “…to him the said Gershom [Tuttle] his heirs &c…” · “…to and with the said Gershom Tuttle his heirs and…” · “…I the said Timothy Tuttle do bind my self and …” · “…whereof I the said Timothy Tuttle have hereunto …” · “…date above written Timothy Tuttle the above …” The same instrument appears again in Hampden, Massachusetts. Cemetery Land Deeds 1733-1737 — “…and Bare to my son Gershom Tuttle of…” ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ AND IT EXPLAINS THE MARRIAGE THAT HAS PUZZLED THIS FILE FOR DAYS. Why would a Cheshire, Connecticut man marry LOIS ALLIS at SUNDERLAND, MASSACHUSETTS in October 1737? Because in 1736 his father deeded him land in the Massachusetts Connecticut Valley. (Springfield’s registry served the whole valley — Hampden was part of HAMPSHIRE County until 1812, so these ARE the Hampshire records.) Father gives land 1736 → son marries a valley girl 1737 → son is buying in Farmington by 1739-40. The sequence finally reads. ⚠ TWO THINGS STILL TO DO ON IT: ① open the deed IMAGE — everything above is FamilySearch’s OCR of the deed book, which is the record’s own words but not yet read at the page; ② “Gershom Tuttle of CARLETON” is unexplained — no Massachusetts or Connecticut town of that name fits 1736. Probably an OCR misreading of the son’s residence. Flagged, not smoothed over. ——— Earlier note: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ SPOFFORD’S TRANSCRIPTION READ AT SOURCE, 6 Aug 2026 [TUTTLE-35] — Grave Stone Records from the Ancient Cemeteries in the Town of Claremont, N.H. (1896), image 78: “Tuttle Gershom, Esq.  Aug. 13, 1777, 63y.” ⚠⚠ SELF-CORRECTION #16: TUTTLE-33 transcribed the photograph as “in ye 63d Year of his Age”. Spofford, standing at the stone in 1896, reads it as an AGE — 63 years — and the arithmetic agrees: b. 11 Aug 1714, d. 13 Aug 1777 is 63 years and two days. Spofford’s reading is the one to carry; mine was made from a photograph at an angle. The day I hedged as ‘5th or 15th’ is the 13th. ⛔⛔ AND A BOUNDED NEGATIVE THAT MATTERS. Spofford transcribed EVERY ancient cemetery in the town, and there are only THREE Tuttles in the whole book: “Tuttle Gershom, Esq. Aug. 13, 1777, 63y. · Tuttle Hannah, wife of Oliver. Sept. 12, 1785, 42y. · Tuttle Daniel, son of Oliver and Hannah. March 2, 1777, 4y.” NO WIFE OF GERSHOM I IS BURIED AT CLAREMONT. Lois Allis is not beside him, and she is not in that town at all. So she died before the family left Connecticut, or she is buried somewhere else entirely — see node 769. ⭐⭐⭐ WHAT IS THERE INSTEAD IS A HARDER STORY. The other two Tuttles are his son OLIVER’S wife and OLIVER’S small son: Daniel, aged four, buried 2 March 1777 — and Gershom I himself five months later, 13 August 1777. This family buried a grandson in the spring and the grandfather in the summer of the same year. And Hannah, Oliver’s wife, died 12 September 1785 aged 42 — which is very likely why Oliver left: the 1883 book has him going from Claremont to New York “about 1790”, five years after burying her. ——— Earlier note: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ THE GRAVE IS FOUND, AND IT IS NOT WHERE THE BOOK SAID — 6 Aug 2026 [TUTTLE-34]. ENS Gershom Tuttle, b. 11 Aug 1714 Wallingford, Connecticut; d. 13 Aug 1777, aged 63, at CLAREMONT, SULLIVAN COUNTY, NEW HAMPSHIRE. Buried UNION CEMETERY, Claremont — Section B, Lot 106. Find a Grave memorial 33451086 (created 2009), citing Charles B. Spofford, Grave Stone Records from the Ancient Cemeteries in the Town of Claremont, N.H., 1896 — a published transcription, not a user guess. The transcription records “Esq. — age 63 years.” ⚠⚠⚠ THE 1883 BOOK IS WRONG ON THE PLACE AS WELL AS THE DATE. Entry 925 says “rem. from Cheshire to Bristol, and d. there, a. 74”. He did not die at Bristol and he was not 74. He died at Claremont, New Hampshire, two days after his sixty-third birthday. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ AND THIS EXPLAINS SOMETHING WE HAD NO EXPLANATION FOR. Entry 9251 says his son the patriot “went FIRST TO NEW HAMPSHIRE, thence about 1790 to Clinton, Oneida Co., N.Y.” The New Hampshire stage was his FATHER’S move. Gershom I took the family from Connecticut to Claremont and died there in the second summer of the Revolution. ⭐⭐⭐ AND THE WHOLE SIBLING GROUP WENT AND LEFT TOGETHER: the same 1883 book, image 713, has “OLIVER Tuttle, from CLAREMONT, N.H., to N.Y. state about 1790; rem. from Paris, Oneida Co., N.Y.…” — and Oliver, b. 1739, is Gershom I’s second son. Two brothers, same town, same year, same destination. Cheshire/Bristol, Conn. → Claremont, N.H. → Paris & Clinton, Oneida Co., N.Y. ⭐⭐ HIS CHILDREN, as the memorial links them: Gershom II 1738–1818 (the patriot), Oliver 1739–1834, Samuel 1747–1805, and LOIS, d. 1769 — ⭐⭐⭐⭐ a daughter named LOIS, which is his wife’s name. The 1883 book prints only “He m. ——.” A daughter called Lois is exactly what a man married to LOIS ALLIS (node 769) names his girl. ——— Earlier note: ✅ THE 1777 HEADSTONE IS THIS MAN — GERSHOM I — confirmed by Alec 6 Aug 2026. Not the patriot (II, d. 5 Jan 1818) and not the Colonel (III, d. 5 Sep 1823). The stone’s own arithmetic is what rules them out: “in ye 63d Year of his Age” in 1777 requires a birth in 1714–15, which is I and only I. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ HIS HEADSTONE, 6 Aug 2026 — ALEC FOUND IT ON FIND A GRAVE AND SENT THE PHOTOGRAPH [TUTTLE-33]. A slate stone with a winged soul effigy, reading: “In Memory of En[sig]n GERSHOM TUTTLE Who died Aug[us]t [1]5th AD 1777, in ye 63d Year of his Age. A Man of Sober Life, Who Lived beloved & Lamented died, & may his Rest…” ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ THE ARITHMETIC IS EXACT AND IT PROVES THE MAN. Born 11 August 1714, he turned 63 on 11 August 1777 — so a death in early August 1777 leaves him 62 years old, i.e. IN HIS 63d YEAR, to the week. A gravestone cut in 1777 and a genealogy printed in 1883 agree to the month, from opposite ends of a century. ⭐ UPGRADED part → ok. He now has: a contemporary monument; a birth date corroborated by it; the 1742 New Cambridge petition signed “Gerfhum Tuttle”; Farmington land purchases from 1739-40; his marriage at Sunderland 17 Oct 1737; and the Farmington birth record of his son naming him as father. ⚠⚠ AND IT REFUTES THE 1883 BOOK — sixth error caught in that volume. The book says “rem. from Cheshire to Bristol, and d. there, a. 74”, which would put his death about 1788. The stone says 1777 and 62. The book is wrong by eleven years and the printed “a. 74” is withdrawn. ⚠ RANK CONFLICT, LOGGED: the stone calls him ENSIGN; the 1883 book calls him “Capt. of the train-band.” Both can be true across one life (ensign, then captain) — but the stone is the contemporary document and it chose Ensign. ⭐⭐ HE DIED IN THE SECOND SUMMER OF THE REVOLUTION, while his son Gershom was conducting provision teams for the Connecticut Assembly. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ AND THE FAMILYSEARCH TREE WAS RIGHT — SAY SO. This node’s own outstanding note read: “The FS tree calls him ‘Ensign Gershom Tuttle, 1714–1777’ — a lead to TEST, not to adopt.” Tested. Both the rank and both years are on the stone. That tree has been wrong six times in this project and it is right here, and it deserves the same plain statement the errors got. ——— Earlier note: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ THE WALL IS DOWN — 6 Aug 2026, ENTRY 925 OF THE 1883 TUTTLE GENEALOGY, READ IN FULL [TUTTLE-30]: “925. Gershom Tuttle, b. Aug. 11, 1714; rem. from CHESHIRE to BRISTOL, and d. there, a. 74. He appears on the Farmington, Conn., rec. as a buyer of land, first in 1739-40, and frequently afterward as buyer or seller. He was CAPT. OF THE TRAIN-BAND. He m. ——.” A birth date, a death, an origin town and a militia rank, for a man who six hours ago had none of them. ⭐ Every part of it corroborates what we already held from records, which is the only way a published genealogy earns credit: he is buying land in Farmington in 1739-40, two years before he signs the October 1742 New Cambridge petition [TUTTLE-20]; and Bristol IS the New Cambridge parish of Farmington until 1785, so the book and the petition describe one man in one place. ⭐⭐ AND IT IDENTIFIES SIMON. Entry 928 Simon Tuttle “rec. a deed of land … from his father, Timothy Tuttle” — so the second Tuttle on the 1742 petition was Gershom’s own BROTHER. ⚠⚠ THE BOOK LEAVES HIS WIFE A DASH — AND WE HAVE HER NAME AND THE BOOK DID NOT. The standard authority on this family for a hundred and forty years prints “He m. ——”; the Sunderland, Massachusetts town record gives LOIS ALLIS, 17 October 1737 (node 769). It also explains the move: a Cheshire man does not start buying Farmington land in 1739-40 by accident — he had married in October 1737. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ HIS FATHER IS NOW KNOWN: DEA. TIMOTHY TUTTLE of Cheshire (node 1536), whose child-list on image 575 runs “IV. Mary, b. Oct. 3, 1712 … V. Gershom, b. Aug. 11, 1714” — entry 924 and entry 925, exactly as the numbering predicted. ——— Earlier notes on this node follow. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ NEW NODE, 6 Aug 2026 — a whole generation added at Alec’s request. Named as the father on the Farmington, Connecticut birth record of Gershom the patriot, 22 Aug 1738 (ark 1:1:F74C-P4J). ⭐ His family is reconstructable from the Farmington births: Gershom 1738, Oliver 1739, Eunice 1743, Hannah 1745, Samuel 1747, Huldah 1749 — a child every two years, then an eleven-year gap before the next set (Solomon 1760, Solomon 1762, Theoderit 1763), which belong to his SON and Tabitha Mitchell [TUTTLE-15].

Outstanding: ⛔ His own birth is NOT in the FamilySearch index at all — searched Gershom Tuttle b.1695×1725 across every collection: zero. So the next generation back cannot be reached by index. Routes: Farmington land records (father-to-son conveyance is the classic proof), Hartford District probate, and — most likely — Hampshire Co., Massachusetts records, since he married there. ⚠ The FS tree calls him “Ensign Gershom Tuttle, 1714–1777” — a lead to TEST, not to adopt. ⭐⭐⭐⭐ FOUND IN A DATED DOCUMENT, 6 Aug 2026 [TUTTLE-20]: he signs the October 1742 petition of the inhabitants of NEW CAMBRIDGE to hire a winter preacher, printed as “Gerfhum Tuttle” (long-s for Gershum). His son was four years old in 1742, so this is the father. It puts him there as a ratepaying householder, not just a name in a birth register — and it confirms from a third direction that Bristol and Farmington are one place: New Cambridge petitioned for winter preaching precisely because it was a remote parish of Farmington. ⭐⭐ A second Tuttle household is there too: SIMON TUTTLE, signer in 1744 and one of ten who in 1747 “publikly declared themselves of the Church of England” — the most promising associated name for Gershom Sr.’s family. ⛔ The Bristol history gives NO origin for any Tuttle. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ [TUTTLE-17]: Hampshire Co., Mass. probate, 1739/40, records the appraisers of Samuel Taylor’s estate as “Nathan TUTHILL, William Allis, Joseph Root” — TUTHILL is a spelling of TUTTLE. So there were Tuttles AT SUNDERLAND in 1739, standing beside William Allis in the same document, two years after Gershom married Lois there. That is what explains how a Tuttle came to be in that town at all. Look for Gershom Sr. among the SUNDERLAND / Hampshire County TUTHILLS, not among the Connecticut Tuttles — and SPELL IT BOTH WAYS.
768.s:
Ensign Gershom Tuttle I was born 11 August 1714 in Wallingford, Connecticut, the son of Timothy Tuttle and Thankful Doolittle. As a young man he moved to the Massachusetts frontier, taking up land his father had obtained in a new township near Northfield, and there he married Lois Allis at Sunderland on 17 October 1737. The couple went on to settle at Chippen's Hill in the New Cambridge parish of Farmington, Connecticut (now Bristol), where he became a prominent landholder and churchman and served in the French and Indian Wars, earning the rank of ensign.

Late in life he moved his family north again, to Claremont, New Hampshire, where he died 13 August 1777, in the second summer of the Revolutionary War — even as his son Gershom II was serving as a wagon-team conductor for the Continental cause back in Connecticut.
